tier_reason: The SIGMOD 2024 paper (open copy at ir.cwi.nl) compares ALP with Zstd, Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, Patas, PDE and Elf. It names the CPU model (Intel Xeon 8375C Ice Lake, Table 3) and the -O3 flags, and the repo sets the compiler (toolchain/i4i_4xlarge.cmake uses clang++, and CMake allows only Clang). The benchmark code is public: publication/source_code/bench_speed, bench_end_to_end (-O3 -march=native -mavx512dq) and bench_compression_ratio, run by publication/script/master_script.sh. That meets tier A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: SIGMOD'24 paper Table 5 (Ice Lake micro-benchmark, tuples per cycle, averaged over all datasets): ALP compresses 14x faster than Zstd, 9x faster than Gorilla, 12x faster than Chimp and Chimp128, 8x faster than Patas, 47x faster than Elf and 251x faster than PDE. It decompresses 26x faster than Zstd, 55x than Gorilla, 66x than Chimp, 65x than Chimp128, 17x than Patas, 215x than Elf and 7x than PDE. Figure 1: '1-2 orders of magnitude faster in [de]compression than all competing schemes'. End-to-end in Tectorwise (Table 6, Figure 6): SCAN and SUM on ALP beat every other scheme and even uncompressed data. City-Temp compression is 4x faster than Patas and 7x faster than Gorilla, and Zstd is 11x slower. Compression ratio (Table 4): ALP averages 21.7 bits/value against Zstd's 20.6, so Zstd is slightly better on average; ALP beats all the other schemes.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang++ (the root CMakeLists allows only Clang; toolchain/i4i_4xlarge.cmake uses /usr/bin/clang++; version not stated). -O3 per the paper. bench_end_to_end CMake adds -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -mavx512dq. Scalar variant: -O3 -fno-slp-vectorize -fno-vectorize. g++ is used only to build the PDE baseline.
corrections.hardware: Main results (Figure 1, Table 5, end-to-end Figure 6 and Table 6) on Intel Ice Lake Xeon 8375C at 3.5 GHz (AWS i4i.4xlarge; the end-to-end run used 16 cores / 32 SMT and 256 GB RAM). Decompression was also run on AMD EPYC 7R13 (Zen3), Apple M1, AWS Graviton2 (Neoverse-N1) and Graviton3 (Paper Table 3).
corrections.caveats: The headline numbers are the authors' own (SIGMOD 2024), backed by the SIGMOD ARI package with all three badges (including Results Reproduced) and the SIGMOD Best Artifact Award. The paper is openly available at ir.cwi.nl/pub/33334/33334.pdf and bronze-OA at ACM. Zstd matches or slightly beats ALP's compression ratio on average (20.6 vs 21.7 bits/value); ALP only wins on ratio when cascaded with other lightweight encodings. The ARI report says the Figure 6 plotting script is missing. The repo CSV publication/end_to_end_bench/result holds raw cycle counts, not ratios.

notes: The record's claim that the paper is paywalled with no preprint is wrong: the CWI repository hosts the full PDF, and I read it. I kept tier A. I replaced the vague claimed_speedup with the Table 5 multipliers and softened the compression-ratio claim against Zstd. The raw end-to-end CSV agrees with the paper: summed cycles show SCAN on ALP about 18-20x cheaper than on Zstd with one thread (derived from page data).

tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed SIGMOD 2023 paper whose text states the claimed 2.6x/3.6x/3.8x decompression gains and the 9x/20x and 5.5x/3.6x/2.8x S3 cost figures against Parquet. It is not A for three reasons: the Parquet/ORC benchmark harness is not in the public repo (only BtrBlocks-side tools/conversion/decompression-speed*.cpp; the engine-comparison code was removed), the paper gives no compiler flags, and the CPU is named only as the 'Xeon Platinum 8000 series (Skylake-SP)' family.

corrections.hardware: AWS c5n.18xlarge: Intel Xeon Platinum 8000 series (Skylake-SP), 36 x 3.5 GHz cores (72 threads, hyperthreading disabled for benchmarks), AVX2/AVX512, 192 GiB RAM, 100 Gbit networking
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.3.1 on Amazon Linux 2, kernel 5.10 (paper). The paper states no optimization flags; the repo CMakeLists adds -march=native -g on top of the CMake build-type defaults.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Public BI in-memory decompression: 2.6x, 3.6x and 3.8x faster than Parquet, Parquet+Snappy and Parquet+Zstd on average. TPC-H in-memory: 2.6x, 3.9x and 4.2x faster. S3 column scans on Public BI are 9x cheaper than compressed Parquet variants and 20x cheaper than uncompressed Parquet on average. Over all 22 TPC-H queries, Parquet, Parquet+Snappy and Parquet+Zstd cost 5.5x, 3.6x and 2.8x more than BtrBlocks.
corrections.caveats: These are the SIGMOD 2023 authors' own measurements. The Parquet/ORC comparison harness and exact build flags are not published; the repo's engine-comparison directory says it was removed because of DeWitt clauses. A later VLDB 2025 paper by competing FastLanes authors (not independent) re-ran BtrBlocks on an AWS i4i.4xlarge. It found BtrBlocks decoded about 7x slower than FastLanes (encoding was 1.37x slower, derived from that paper's Table 4). BtrBlocks gained nothing from AVX512 and could not do single-value random access without an API reimplementation. On compression ratio BtrBlocks was +18% larger than FastLanes on Public BI, versus +2% for Parquet+Zstd.

notes: The numbers are verbatim in the paper. I downgraded A to B because the baseline-side benchmark code, flags and exact CPU model are missing. I also fixed the record's FastLanes-paper caveat: '7x slower encoding' and 'close to Parquet+Zstd compression ratio' are not what that paper shows. Metadata is confirmed: MIT, 289 stars, last commit 2025-04-07 (stale).

tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed VLDB 2025 paper, and its public artifact repo (cwida/fastlanes-vldb2025: master_script.py, scripts/, plus FastLanes CMake targets benchmark_decompression_time and benchmark_random_access) reproduces Tables 3-6 against Parquet, DuckDB and BtrBlocks. It is not A: the paper never names the compiler (the artifact README says 'gcc / clang'), and the CPU is given only as 'Intel Xeon (Ice Lake)' on an i4i.4xlarge with no model number.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Decoding (Table 4, i4i.4xlarge Ice Lake): on average 29x faster than DuckDB's native format, 43x faster than Parquet+Snappy, 44x faster than Parquet+Zstd and 7x faster than BtrBlocks. Totals: 16.32 ms vs 483.45, 712.55, 731.45 and 115.43 ms. Encoding is not faster: FastLanes v0.1 took 81,341.63 ms against 5,867.07 (Parquet+Snappy), 6,927.52 (Parquet+Zstd) and 20,347.82 (DuckDB). That makes it about 14x, 12x and 4x slower, and only about 1.4x faster than BtrBlocks (111,091.39 ms) (derived from page data). Random access (Table 5; text says 315x/416x/800x/5x): first-value retrieval takes 0.14 ms, 315.62x faster than Parquet+Snappy, 413.66x than Parquet+Zstd, 813.57x than BtrBlocks and 5.96x than DuckDB.
corrections.baseline: Apache Parquet (Snappy and Zstd variants, written and read with DuckDB v1.2's Parquet implementation) and DuckDB v1.2's native storage format; also BtrBlocks
corrections.hardware: All experiments on AWS EC2 i4i.4xlarge: Intel Xeon (Ice Lake), 16 vCPUs, 128 GiB RAM (paper Sec. 4; no CPU model number given). Only the expression-pool micro-benchmark (Table 7, footnote 4) ran on an Apple MacBook Pro M4.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: The paper does not name the compiler (the artifact README lists 'gcc / clang'; the current FastLanes CMakeLists defaults to clang++ on non-Windows). FastLanes is built as a CMake Release. The SIMD micro-benchmark (Table 6) used -O3, -O3 -mavx2 and -O3 -mavx512dq.
corrections.caveats: These are the authors' own VLDB 2025 numbers (Afroozeh & Boncz, CWI). The artifact repo cwida/fastlanes-vldb2025 reproduces them. Parquet was run through DuckDB v1.2's Parquet reader and writer, not parquet-cpp/Arrow. The headline multipliers are decoding-only: FastLanes v0.1 encoding is 4-14x slower than DuckDB and Parquet and beats only BtrBlocks, which the authors attribute to an unoptimized encoder. Random access was simulated with LIMIT 1 queries on Parquet and DuckDB and with full block decoding for BtrBlocks. The table and text multipliers differ slightly (413.66x vs 416x, 813.57x vs 800x).

notes: The record's '29x faster decoding/encoding' is overstated: the Table 4 multipliers are for decoding, and FastLanes encoding is slower than Parquet and DuckDB. The record also put Table 5 on the M4, but the M4 footnote belongs to the Table 7 expression-pool experiment. Metadata is confirmed: MIT, 713 stars, last commit 2026-04-22 (active, dev branch).
